candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — integrate advance directives into client plan of care
candidate.educational_objective: Explain that a capable patient retains healthcare decision-making authority and a healthcare agent acts when the patient cannot, subject to applicable law.

options.A: “Yes. Naming an agent transfers healthcare decision-making authority immediately after the advance directive is signed and witnessed.”
options.B: “Yes. The agent becomes the primary decision-maker now; you keep authority only for choices the directive does not address.”
options.C: “No. You continue making your own healthcare decisions while you have capacity; the agent speaks for you when you cannot do so.”
options.D: “No. The agent can make decisions now once the hospital activates the directive under its policy, even while you retain capacity.”

candidate.rationale: An advance directive is intended to guide care or identify a surrogate when the person cannot make or communicate healthcare decisions. Naming a healthcare agent does not replace the decisions of a client who currently has decision-making capacity. Requirements for valid advance directives and activation details vary by state, so the nurse should avoid implying that facility preference alone determines authority.
candidate.source_claim_supported: A patient who retains decision-making capacity continues to make their own healthcare decisions; a designated healthcare agent speaks when the patient cannot, subject to applicable law.

candidate.stem: A client with decision-making capacity is completing an advance directive and asks, “If I name my sister as my healthcare agent, does she start making decisions for me now?” Which response by the nurse is best?
